newsitem.title: USA: Summit leaders warn Balkan leaders, IRA.
newsitem.headline: Summit leaders warn Balkan leaders, IRA.

text.p: Leaders of the world's rich nations and Russia warned Bosnia's former warring parties on Saturday they could face a cut-off in aid if they let the peace process falter.

"We are prepared to continue to help the states of this region, but our continued commitment is not unconditional," the leaders said in a draft statement to be approved on the second day of the Group of Seven's annual summit.
A suspected Irish Republican Army bomb explosion in central Belfast on Saturday intruded on the leaders as they took up the issue of fighting terrorism.
President Bill Clinton and British Prime Minister Tony Blair condemned the blast and told the IRA's political wing Sinn Fein violence would have to end if they wanted to join peace talks.

Russian President Boris Yeltsin joined the leaders of G7 members the United States, France, Britain, Germany, Italy, Canada and Japan in reviewing world problems, such as Africa and international terrorism, around a table at the Denver Public Library in what was dubbed "The Summit of the Eight".

The Bosnia statement sidestepped the touchy issue of whether the NATO peace-keeping force in Bosnia would be withdrawn as scheduled in June 1998, on which the United States and European leaders are at odds.
"We support the mission of the stabilisation force to help provide a secure environment by June 1998," it said.

The Europeans have voiced concern to Clinton about plans to withdraw the 8,500-strong U.S. contingent from the 31,000-strong force on schedule next year because they fear it could undermine the force and prompt bloodshed.
Clinton resisted pressure at a dinner on Friday night, saying the allies must concentrate on buttressing the peace process in Bosnia.

The leaders said they were dissatisfied with progress in implementing portions of the 1995 Dayton Peace Accords requiring refugees to be allowed to go home and respect for human rights and democratic bodies.
"Further progress towards European and international institutions wll depend on improvements in these areas," they said.
Summit leaders gave a warm welcome to Yeltsin, who only a year ago was fighting for his life from heart problems but is now back to his old ebullient self.

"I want to say a special welcome to our friend President Yeltsin, who joins us for the first time from the beginning to the end of this meeting. Russia's growing role in the shared world of market democracies reflects the progress and the potential of this age," Clinton said.

A draft copy of the final communique to be released on Sunday said Russia's presence "marks a new and deeper participation by Russia in our efforts" and praised Moscow for having taken "bold measures to complete its historic transformation into a market democracy."

But it did not say that Russia was now a full member of what would be a Group of Eight. France said there was a consensus among the leaders to keep Russia out of discussions on international financial issues.
Yeltsin is excluded from only one summit meeting later Saturday on international economic and financial matters.
The final communique said the leaders opposed human cloning and urged national reconciliation in Cambodia, where former dictator Pol Pot is reported to have been captured.

It said that their aid to the Democratic Republic of the Congo, which was Zaire until President Mobutu Sese Seko was toppled, would depend on democratic reform, including elections and respect for human rights.
The official harmony masked European resentment at what some considered U.S. lecturing at a summit where Clinton was basking in the glow of a booming economy.
"The Americans were saying look how good we are and look how bad you are," sniffed one delegation source after a finance ministers' meeting on Friday.

A G7 source said the leaders would call in an economic statement to be released later on Saturday for continued cooperation on macro-economic policies and foreign exchange. They would also welcome introduction of the new European currency, the euro, according to a draft of the statement.
The United States had to remain vigilant against resurgence of inflation and Britain should must keep inflation under control, it said.
